newsitem.title: USA: Swiss used "Jewish assets" to pay citizens - D'Amato.
newsitem.headline: Swiss used "Jewish assets" to pay citizens - D'Amato.

text.p: Claiming that Swiss citizens "benefitted from the Holocaust," the head of the Senate Banking Committee on Wednesday said the Swiss government used Jewish assets to compensate its own citizens for properties taken from them in communist East Europe.

New York Republican Alfonse D'Amato made his comments at an emotionally charged hearing in which Holocaust survivors wept in recalling how Swiss banks refused to help them track family bank accounts -- demanding that they produce death certificates for people who perished in Nazi death camps.

D'Amato, whose committee has been probing the Swiss financial role in the Second World War, said newly discovered documents showed the Swiss were bigger collaborators with the Nazis than previously imagined. He accused Switzerland of stalling justice by setting up a commission that will take five years to report its findings on the amount of looted assets deposited by Germans in their Swiss safe haven.

The senator said researchers had recently uncovered documents showing that the Swiss, in a secret 1949 deal with Poland, used assets of Polish Jews to compensate Swiss citizens for the nationalisation of their property in the then-Communist country. He said that similar deals were struck later with Hungary and Czechoslovakia.
"What we have here is a situation where the Swiss turned over assets that belonged to the Jews of Poland to settle claims made by Swiss citizens," D'Amato said.

An aide to D'Amato told Reuters the Jewish assets used to compensate Swiss citizens were on deposit in Swiss banks -- coming from Jews who sought to protect their wealth by establishing secret bank accounts in neutral Switzerland.
"The (the Swiss government) enriched Swiss citizens. ... Swiss citizens benefitted from the Holocaust," D'Amato said.

U.S. documents made public at the hearing showed that American officials were worried by the Swiss agreement with Poland in 1949 whereby assets of Polish nationals who died without heirs would be turned over to Poland's government.

D'Amato said other newly discovered documents showed that the Germans, during the war, invested between $414 million and $816 million in Swiss enterprises and sold the Swiss hundreds of millions of dollars in looted gold.
But after the war, Switzerland admitted to having only $250 million in German assets and kept half for itself while compensating the allies with $125 million.
D'Amato said that the Swiss also shortchanged the allies on the looted gold -- giving them only $60 million of what was really worth hundreds of million of dollars.
Nobel Peace Prize winner Elie Wiesel, a survivor of two Nazi death camps, told the hearing Switzerland had much to answer for because of its conduct in the war.

"Switzerland did save some Jewish lives but how is one to explain that the very idea of stamping German passports with a 'J' for Jewish came not from Germany but from Switzerland? How is one to explain that Switzerland collaboated with German agents to keep Jewish money in their safes? Why did it take so long for this to come out?" he asked.
